questions.q: What does factoring N reduce to in Shor's algorithm?
options: Finding the multiplicative order r of a randomly chosen a coprime to N -- the smallest r > 0 with a^r ≡ 1 (mod N)
Directly guessing the two prime factors by trial division
Finding the largest prime less than N
Computing N's square root to arbitrary precision
questions.explain: The entire reduction hinges on period-finding: once the order r of a mod N is known, the factors of N can be recovered with classical arithmetic.

questions.q: Why does the algebraic identity a^r - 1 = (a^(r/2) - 1)(a^(r/2) + 1) require r to be even?
options: r/2 must be a whole number for the difference-of-squares factorization to apply, which is only guaranteed when r is even
It doesn't require r to be even; the identity holds for any r
Even numbers are always prime factors of N
The identity only applies when a itself is an even number
questions.explain: The difference-of-squares step treats a^r as (a^(r/2))^2 - 1, which needs r/2 to be an integer -- hence the evenness requirement.

questions.q: In the worked example N = 15, a = 7, what is the computed order r, and what are the two gcd results?
Why does a nontrivial gcd result require a^(r/2) to be not congruent to -1 (mod N), in addition to r being even?
options: If a^(r/2) ≡ -1 (mod N), then a^(r/2) - 1 and a^(r/2) + 1 become N-2 and N respectively in residue terms, and the gcds collapse to trivial divisors (1 and N) instead of real factors
The -1 condition is unnecessary; evenness of r alone always guarantees nontrivial factors
a^(r/2) must equal exactly N/2 for the gcds to work
The -1 condition only matters when N is even
questions.explain: When a^(r/2) ≡ -1 (mod N), one gcd term becomes congruent to 0 mod N in a way that forces a trivial gcd -- this is the documented failure mode explored numerically with a = 14 for N = 15.

questions.q: What is the proven probabilistic guarantee for randomly chosen a, and what does it imply about retries?
options: For N a product of two distinct odd primes, a random a coprime to N has probability at least 1/2 of giving an even r with a^(r/2) not congruent to -1 (mod N), so on average about two attempts suffice
Every randomly chosen a is guaranteed to succeed on the first attempt with probability 1
The probability of success is always exactly 1/4 regardless of N
Retrying with a new a never changes the outcome, since the result is deterministic
questions.explain: This is a proven theorem bounding the success probability at 1/2 or better per random a, which is why Shor's algorithm is a randomized algorithm with a cheap retry step, not a single deterministic pass.
